description: Candidate terms extracted from every skill's front matter: `name` as the label, `description` as the definition. Generated by folio-assistant-core/scripts/glossary-extract.ts; not curated, and never hand-edited: a person promotes a term by authoring it in a glossary of their own.

terms.definition: Settle a review that reached no mechanical or consensus agreement. What makes a disagreement adjudicable, the shape its implementations share, why the adjudication LEADS the criterion while the checker's entry is kept beneath it, and the dispensation that records the reason — scoped to a version, never precedent.

The general process for turning a shared paper, book or standard into an adopted methodology: establish origin and licence, ingest the source, find and summarize related work items and issues and ask whether to coordinate, render the method with its adopted and refused parts, place it by ownership, integrate it by calling existing processes, give every tool it uses a Tool node, and put it to the owner. Process: processes/library/methodology-from-source.bpmn.

Review a pull request an agent touched by building the strongest case that it is wrong, unsafe, or not what it claims, and record the verdict where the merge gate reads it: one `merge-review/v1` file per head, on the `merge-reviews` state branch, never in the pull request itself. Covers who may review, what the whole-diff scope is, the RED FLAG categories and their evidence rule, the one rebuttal round, overrides, and how a per-head verdict composes with a merge train.

Governs handing ONE task to an agent in another environment — a local agent with network the cloud session lacks, a sibling on a different machine, anything that cannot read the coordinator's context and that a person may relay to. States who writes which work item, where the receiver reports, what the person pastes (one sentence: work item, branch, repository) and the brief the work item opens with (second person, to the executor), what the receiver checks before acting, who closes, who may grant an exception, and how to recognise and answer the five ways an executor fails. Use when writing a work item for another agent to execute, and as the receiver before acting on one. Triggers on: hand off, handoff, local agent, agy, mac agent, needs network, executor failed, agent went silent, re-hand, "give me a branch and bean for them", relay, the other agent.

Durable memory for a subagent — the three entry labels and what each promises, why entries are authored as graph nodes rather than in the generated file, the injection budget that silently truncates, and archiving as the third state between "reaches everybody" and "deleted".

Securing what a coding agent may do without asking, from the person who can grant it: the `secure-agent-permissions` sub-process, run at session start and on demand when an action is denied. Vendor-neutral: the coding agent is a Tool (Claude Code is one; Gemini CLI, Cursor, Copilot and Codex are others), and each Tool's own config format belongs to its adapter, not here. Covers the permissions the harness's processes need, least privilege, how each one is explained before it is granted, how a grant is recorded, and the rules that no grant relaxes: never self-granted, generated projections are CI's, and merging to main is never a standing permission.

ArchiMate models as knowledge-graph content: how an instance declares the Archi models it holds, what the `archimate` subgraph gives every model, view, element and relationship (an IRI, a thin page, and every view drawn as SVG from the model's own diagram, and its metamodel derived and checked), how to version the models, how to wire them into a folio's staging build and navbar, how to count and lower the crossed lines in a view before committing it, why every view carries a plain-language key, why names are the source's own terms linked to their SKOS concepts, and why no Java, no Archi CLI and no Archi HTML report is ever part of the pipeline. Read before adding, authoring, publishing or rendering an `.archimate` file, before citing an ArchiMate element from prose, and before reaching for Archi's own tooling in CI.

Which declared executable artefacts can be reached — decision tables, BPMN diagrams, self-declared entry points. Read before trusting that a .dmn works because it loads, before concluding a script has a caller, and before building any reachability report: load is not evaluability, a test is not a caller, and where a grep fails in both directions the subject has to be narrowed rather than the signals.

Put one question or decision to a person: the full question, context and every option written in the chat FIRST, then the same options as a tappable card. Use before every AskUserQuestion, request_decision / Decision card, button card, or any ask that hands a choice to the owner. Input is the composed question; output is the answer, or the default taken.

Reading a container — a zip, a PDF, a saved web page — into the knowledge graph. What goes in by default (metadata), what does not (contents), the three timestamps that sit near each other and mean different things, and why a producer string is evidence.
Declare a harness this one knows about and does not hold (`associatedHarnesses`): a folio in another repository, published at its own site. Referenced, never loaded, never materialized.

Which audits reach which KIND of node, measured rather than inferred. Read before concluding that a corpus is unaudited, before writing a criterion for one, and before building any coverage report — the gate half must be declared, an undeclared declarer is counted, and the stored record holds the relation rather than the census.

Derived documentation for a sub-graph — what the handler emits, what it deliberately does not, and the obligation on whoever authors a harness's docs: summarise what the index lists, by reusing it rather than restating it.

Default to non-blocking when updating a work item's status. Mark blocked only when the work genuinely cannot proceed, and then always with what it waits on, when the wait expires, and what the next agent should do.

Pointer to the bean-based session work-plan system (the `beans` CLI flat-file issue tracker, data under `beans/`). Operational usage lives in todo-manager.md / session-intent.md; this file is the canonical copy of the coordinator logic that downstream repositories sync from.

Drain open work items (stories, bugs, features) with several agents at once, as part of the SDLC: build the queue, group it by owner, check and claim each work item on every work item copy before any work, open the PR at the first commit, ask the owner through ask-the-person, close, and refill. Use when a thread or agent is asked to drain work items, when a coordinator spawns drain threads, or when an idle agent pulls from a shared queue next to other agents.

Make a reviewer-facing BEFORE/AFTER preview of a change to anything that is rendered — a docs site, a paper's PDF, a FHIR IG, a slide deck, a website — and put it where the review and feedback processes expect it. Covers one build with one variable, stable capture, pairing every picture with a measured count and its method, the viewports and colour schemes to shoot, an honest status line, publishing with alt text, a section per content type naming this repository's own build and render tools, and how reviewer feedback on the preview becomes work items. Use before asking anyone to review a rendered change, at the HCI validation gate, and whenever a reviewer asks "what did it look like before".

Benchmarking output is a synthesized report across models and configurations, deliberately excluded from declared knowledge-graph typologies. Contrast with QA review mode, where reports land (build/benchmarks/ or reports/), and path guards preventing benchmark data from polluting the knowledge graph.

Audits individual content blocks for single-topic coherence, length, and embedded tables. Blocks that cover multiple topics or exceed ~2/3 of a page should be split; large tables (>5 rows) must be their own `table` block. Child blocks from a split may belong in different chapters than the parent.

A build or a model download fails from an agent container. Read which of three different refusals it is before doing anything — a policy denial (403 on CONNECT), an upstream rate limit (429), or a host that is simply down — because each has a different remedy. Covers the Maven Central mirror that gets a Gradle or Maven build through a 429, which hosts were measured open and shut, and when the work belongs to an agent with different network access instead.
A board is a DIAGRAM OF a folio, not a container of one. The OMG split between the semantic model and its layout, why the arrow runs one way, and what a note may never carry.
Everything starts as its avatar; opening projects a window onto the board. The two mechanisms that must not be conflated, z-order, and the fixed chrome a content kind fills in.

Make a BPMN diagram readable at 100% without zooming, and untangle it: keep it inside the size budget, give every label a place clear of other labels, flows and boxes, remove crossings, and swap lanes when another order makes the flows between lanes shorter. Run before and after every diagram edit.

Every process here is BPMN, the diagrams are executable, and the base processes are strict. How to author one, how to run it, how a package relaxes a step and what it may never relax, and which gateways are computed rather than chosen.

Classify every remote branch against the default branch (merged, landed by squash or cherry-pick, partially landed, unlanded, undetermined) by commit ancestry, patch-id and merge-tree, not by subject line. Report only, never delete. A branch touching content or mathematics is a salvage-review item and never a delete candidate. Covers the treeless fetch that makes thousands of branches cheap, caching by tip sha, and the report's shape. Read before answering "which branches can go?" or "what work never landed?".

Read what changed on main often, and re-analyse the session workplan. Put main INTO the branch rarely: freely before a PR exists, and on a branch with a PR only when it conflicts, when the work needs something that just landed, or once just before it merges, because each such push re-runs the PR's whole CI. Prevents stale assumptions, merge conflicts, and duplicated work without spending CI on churn.

How Bun is used as the JavaScript/TypeScript execution runtime, test runner, package manager, and tarball packager across separated repositories: standalone subgraph configuration (bunfig.toml, package.json, tsconfig.json), test preloads, dependency resolution without rootDir pitfalls, packaging with bun pm pack, and coordinator vs standalone execution models.

Every CI step is a pure function of its inputs: derive the inputs, hash them into a key, restore on a hit, run and save on a miss. Read before adding a cache to a workflow, before writing a cache key, before trusting a restored output or a skipped verdict, and before pushing a change that moves a cached step's key. Covers the one primitive (`cached-step` + `cache:key`), the trust classes, what a committer publishes, the 10 GB budget, and the hit-rate report.

Derivation-discipline integration watcher — watches the default branch + open active PRs + newly-opened PRs for non-canonical empirical / fitting / calibration inputs beyond the project's declared set, numerology, or justification/rationalization in place of derivation. Inherits shared mechanics (Monitor, subscriptions, queue, ledger, idle sweep, author-ask, watch-prepared-PRs, witness-drift recovery, billing-quick-fail flake, post-completion one-voice, sibling-PR comment protocol, backlog-found PR spin-up, handover docs) from `sdlc-core/integration-watcher`.

The change-size rule: keeps review increments adjudicable by establishing a line-count threshold (~400 effective lines), recording its empirical basis, weighting prose/KG lower than code, and distinguishing size from complexity.

Analyse a chapter's internal dependency graph to find backward edges (blocks that reference something defined later), compute graph energy, and suggest section/block reorderings that minimise complexity. Uses Graphviz for visualisation and brute-force permutation search for optimal section ordering.

A red workflow looks exactly like a green one from inside a checkout. How to read a default-branch health report, the three verdicts that keep it honest, why a watchdog needs both a session-start print and an unattended run, and the separate external question the Pages deployments need.

Author, extend or consume a code list: a closed set of codes, each with a label, a definition and a source, kept as a node and published as SKOS. Use when a diagram, a schema or a script needs a fixed set of values (adjudication answers, namespace IRIs) instead of strings in code.

Review the knowledge graph's CODE nodes — Tool definitions in the `tools` graph and schema definition nodes under `schemas/` — for the joins a reader cannot see: that a node declares what it is, that what it names resolves, and that the mechanism it describes is the one that actually runs.

Where code review sits in the release lifecycle. Review types, who reviews what, how feedback maps to work items, and the path from review to approval to release. Works with prepare-merge-auto for mechanics and release-lifecycle for the broader flow.

Determine the language an agent SPEAKS IN — the language of a turn, as against the language of content. Covers the four inputs and their order, why a model's own languages are never the answer, the boundary between speaking to the person and writing durable artefacts, where the determination is recorded so a sibling session does not re-ask, and when to re-ask.

The general pattern for caching expensive compiled artefacts (Lean .oleans, FHIR ASTs) across builds. Defines branch-based storage, validity checking, exit code protocol, safety guards, and the restore→build→contribute loop.

A human may waive a confirmation they are owed — for a session, for a process run, or until a stated time. Covers what a waiver is made of, where it is recorded (the context graph, never the work plan), the gates that can be waived and the rules that cannot, why every waiver carries an expiry, and the one thing an agent may never do: grant itself one.

Getting a resource INTO the graph in the first place — accepting one offered unprompted, or asking for one and then asking for it to be uploaded. The channels are plural and open: `uploads/` is one, the conversation is another. Runs before document ingestion, which begins only once a file has landed.

Every declared graph is the subject a process produces, static context it reads, or live state it writes. The one question that settles it, the classification of every kind with its reason, what a consumer may assume of each layer, and why agent memory is context rather than state.

Editorial graph analysis skill — builds a content graph from uses[], interprets, proofs, and examples relationships; builds a chapter/section topology graph; and applies heuristics to identify forward references, cross-section/cross-chapter coupling, and sections that are too sparse or too dense. Produces actionable reorganisation suggestions and can implement approved moves.

Adapters and profiles are different axes and conflating them is costly. What a document folio is, how a paper extends it, which distinction needs code and which needs only rules, and what profile enforcement catches that schema validation structurally cannot.

Make in-flight work trackable by others in real time — open a PR from the first commit, push small coherent increments continuously (never hoard uncommitted work), keep a live status checklist in the PR body, and post brief intent on the PR + any overlapping sibling PRs. Use on any multi-step or long-running task, especially when siblings/agents or the author may need to follow, cherry-pick, or take over mid-flight.

Coordinate work across multiple in-flight Claude PRs working toward a shared goal. Post intent + asks on related PRs, identify cherry-pickable work, respond to code-review comments on your own PR, periodically triage sibling PR activity (new comments, CI status, new commits), watch main + newly created branches/PRs, escalate inconsistent findings to the author, and keep a coordination ledger up to date.
Materialized content is read-only. To work on it you take a copy into your own folio/, and the copy records what it is a copy of — the local-provenance edge, which is not the upstream one.

Pre-declaration corpus check. Before declaring any item "open", "gap", "TODO", "open problem", "pending derivation" — or asserting in chat that something is unresolved in the corpus — run the four-path grep checklist. A source file's `## Status` note lags the corpus by weeks; the corpus is the source of truth. An item is open only after all four paths come back empty (modulo the originating file itself).

A skill can be satisfied by the neighbours of its mechanism while the mechanism is reachable from no Tool node. Read before concluding from check:tools that a command is reachable, and before adding a Tool node or a `maintains` claim.

The CRDM data-modelling phase — when in the requirements process a model is built, what it is built from, who confirms it, and what it hands to the phases either side. The technique it invokes is `data-modelling`; this skill carries only the sequencing and the sign-off.
Detect when a request needs requirements agreed before anything is built, and which of the two parallel requirements methodologies governs it.

Guide for CRDM Phase 4 — Impact Analysis and Migration Planning. Systematic scan across 7 dimensions: schema, pipeline, adapter, folio, skill, migration, and test/documentation impact. Produces a structured assessment for posting to the GitHub issue.

Facilitate Phase 1 (Needs Assessment) of the CRDM requirements workflow. Guide the BA through stakeholder identification, source material gathering, and synthesising a domain-language needs statement. Post to the GitHub issue and iterate until the BA confirms the need is correctly captured.

Turn a recorded requirements walkthrough (a video call where a business analyst demonstrates a feature and a stakeholder asks for changes) into CRDM Phase 3 requirements with evidence: transcripts compared, an independent transcript where one can be made, screenshots cut at the moments the speakers point at the screen, and every requirement traced to a timestamp. Use when someone uploads a meeting recording, a Teams/Zoom transcript (.vtt, .docx) or both, and asks for requirements from it.
Guide and template for CRDM Phase 3 — Requirements Definition. Helps the agent structure requirements from conversation using a REQ-### format with acceptance criteria, priority, and traceability.
Draft a sticky note from the conversation, choose its theme and its place, preview it, and only then attach it to a node.

Build a data model: identify the entities a body of work is actually about, the relations between them, and the cardinalities — then declare it where the tools can read it. Process-agnostic technique; the CRDM phase that invokes it is `crdm-data-model`.

Record why a decision was made, or why a finding in it was left. Required of whoever adjudicates a gate, and of the agent that assembles the citations for them. Every overrule of a mechanical finding carries a note, and every note cites corpus evidence.

Lay a decision out as a comparison before you ask it — what each option does, its pro, its con, what it changes downstream, and how reversible it is — in the prose that precedes the question, never inside the option labels. Required whenever a choice is handed to a person.

Given a decision context, select the applicable methodology from the methodology graph. Reads the graph's applies-when declarations, matches them against the context, and returns the ranked applicable methods with rationale. Extends methodology-adoption's four-question protocol with quantitative method-selection criteria from the MCDM literature.

An agent never removes a durable artefact on its own initiative. Report what would go, with sizes and ages, and wait for the user to say so. Covers what counts as durable, the non-destructive move for each kind, and the rule that a workflow whose shape deletes something counts as a deletion nobody decided.
Post-delivery summary with server restart command and viewer links

The agent must know its UI surface — gh-pages, local server, with/without MCP, or chat discussion only — because deployment surfaces are declared architectural facts that decide which tools apply, forbid request-time assumptions, and require graceful degradation to chat.

Workflow processing is a SPECTRUM, not a switch. The four mechanisms this repository uses to sit at different points on it, the four axes an answer has to name, what is measured today, and the three research questions — which are open, and marked as open.

Logical devil's-advocate integration watcher — for every content block (.ts/.md) and formal sibling, constructs the strongest adversarial case that it is WRONG: the objection a hostile-but- competent referee would raise (false claim, vacuity, circularity, overclaim, hidden degree-of-freedom, logical non-sequitur, formal↔narrative divergence, citation misuse, definitional ambiguity, empirical fragility, domain implausibility, irreproducible compute). Fans out multiple adversarial-lens agents per block, then an adjudicator scores whether each objection survives rebuttal. Persists per-block <block>.qa.json entries under the `da-*` criteria family (reviewer.kind = "agent"). Operationalizes the standing Critical-distance red-team license (AGENTS.md). Inherits all shared mechanics (Monitor, subscriptions, queue, ledger, idle sweep, author-ask, watch-prepared-PRs, witness-drift recovery, billing-quick-fail flake) from `integration-watcher`.
Show per-block content changes with viewer links, changelog, and undo impact analysis

Dispatch one or more background sub-agents against parallel research/build fronts with a STANDARDIZED live progress contract, and monitor them on a 2-minute heartbeat. Every dispatched agent emits consistent DID/DOING/NEXT/BLOCKERS blocks with real log output (not static "still running"); the parent extracts the latest block from each agent every ~120 s and posts one consolidated synthesis table. Use when the user says "dispatch agents", "fan out", "run these in parallel with monitoring", "give me status every 2 minutes", or when you are about to launch ≥ 2 background Agents on independent work.

How a checkout of this harness generates and publishes its docs site: regenerating derived references, composing the docs layers and each instance's site into one Jekyll source, building it with just-the-docs, the post-build passes, the TypeDoc API reference, the knowledge-graph export, and the full-replace publish to gh-pages and its branches/ previews.
How a domain-specific rule is kept out of the platform without being lost — the opt-in axis mechanism, why a profile is not a fence, and the test for whether a rule generalizes at all.

A graph has more than one kind of edge, and conflating them corrupts both the ordering and the impact answer. Interface edges versus implementation edges, the union rule for blast radius, and the split/merge signals — generalized out of the formal-math skills that first stated them.

Evidence review as an instance of untainted verification — the separation of the appraising party from the drafting party, what recurring surveillance in a living guideline shares with a stale QA verdict, and which of guideline methodology's rules are fenced rather than shipped.

Drain the paper's narrative blocks through an exposition-quality swarm: a small fleet of grouped-batch agents each audit their batch against the Milnor exposition gate (expo-milnor-clarity, H1–H8) plus the deterministic narrative defect checks (proof-sketch-vs-kind, proof-no-lean-mention-in-prose, proof-cross-block-duplication), then RESOLVE the flagged blocks with conservative, math-preserving edits. Each swarm agent owns its own branch (commits, pushes, opens a PR); the foreground session runs auto prepare-merge on each swarm branch and repeats batch-by-batch until the paper is completely drained. Sister to `/integration-backlog` (that drains watcher findings; this drains exposition quality).

The contract the `external-registry` role is held to: what a trusted registry outside this instance must provide for a portal to verify what it received, and what the verifier does when it cannot. The narrowest contract the diagrams require. A mechanical role's skill is a contract to test against, not instructions to read.

Manages feature-branch staging deployments under gh-pages/branches/<branch-slug>/ for before/after publication review comparison. Handles branch creation, staging deployment, commit SHA stamping, and cleanup.

A script needs a program or module the container does not have (tesseract, pdftoppm, PyMuPDF, a CLI from a GitHub release). Get it: `bun run cat software:ensure`, which tries apt, pip, then a pinned and checksummed GitHub release, from the declared table `scripts/software.json`. Do not route around a missing tool with a cache, a weaker backend or a skipped step, and do not report "not installed" as if it were a finding about the work.

A flushable container is a named store that accumulates by design — a trash you can recover from, a review preview, a console log. It declares a buffer limit, badges when over it, and offers three flush actions: flush all, trim to limit, and select to prune. What "flush" means, and which end of the order is expendable, are declared per container and differ.

Scaffold a new folio instance from the harness — the instantiate affordance of the knowledge graph. Covers when to run folio-init vs remote-mount, what the scaffold writes, the builder shim, state branch seeding, write capability requirements, and --dry-run degradation.

Reading `bun run cat gates`' "NOT clean" verdict. Why every gate can pass and the run still exit 1, the two causes and how to tell them apart in one command, and the question that settles whether a churning field is a defect in the writer: does it describe the SUBJECT or the RUN?

You have a fix. Before it ships, ask what CLASS of defect it belongs to and whether the fix sits at the right layer — then attack your own answer: name what the fix now catches that the bug did not. Two axes go wrong, SCOPE and STATE, and widening either past the problem is how a fix becomes the next defect. Applies to a bug fix, a schema change, a detector, or a claim in a paper. Use after the fix works and before the pull request.

Triage what a person means when they ask to create a folio, and route them. Five requests share one sentence — a folio in a new repo, folio-assistant overlaid on an existing repo, a second folio in an instance that already has one, a content object they called a folio, or something the filesystem cannot tell apart. Reads the repository facts, runs them through the folio-intent decision table, asks a selectable question for what facts cannot settle, scaffolds, and reports the published URL. Use whenever a user asks to create, start, set up, or initialise a folio, a paper, a DAK, an IG, or "folio-assistant" itself.

Answer questions about GitHub-hosted state — is a page published, where does it live, did CI pass, does a branch exist — by reading the ref or the API, never by composing a URL or fetching one. The first check for any deployment or 404 question is `git ls-tree` of the publish ref.

Cold start, then review a time window of activity — sibling sessions, the work plan, issues, change proposals, branches, CI — and prioritise what it finds against goals stated in the owner's words. Inputs are the window, the goals, the scope and the axes; the output is a synopsis (closed, open, needs doing, with effort), a priority queue per goal with selectable next actions, and the instruction gaps met on the way, each recorded as a work item. Use when asked "what happened", "what is stalled", "what should we do next for X", or at the start of a session that inherits parallel work.

Drive a tangled graph toward a clean partition, so a sub-graph can be split off when it grows too large or when a business reason separates it. The staged practice — declare in place, detangle, isolate, extract — and the seventeen moves for measurement, ordering, judgement and enforcement.

Draw any graph in a harness (schemas, processes, a folio's block graph and any formal relation its content type adds, a detangle partition) so the picture is derived, checkable and readable. Ten rules, which engine to lay a graph out with and why, and how each graph typology here applies them.

A sibling agent, spawned during or working beside a live agent-human discussion, hands every card, question, decision, result, blocker or piece of context back to the discussion agent that is talking with the person, and never leaves it only in its own thread. The discussion agent asks the person (ask-the-person), marks every copy answered, and routes the answer back. A review sheet or issue in play is an extra channel. Use whenever an agent that is not the one talking with the person has something the person must see.

Write a handover report: a templated snapshot of an agent's current state, committed as a work item note, so that a session or subagent that stalls, runs out of context, or loses its container can be picked up by another agent without re-deriving anything. Use it when you are told a stall is likely, at the end of every long arc, before a risky or long-running step, and whenever a steward asks for one. Its reader is `stalled-agent-triage`.

Who may write under `.claude/`, and when. The generated projections of the knowledge graph (`.claude/commands/*.md` from `skill:commands`, the assembled agent memory under `.claude/agents/` and `.claude/agent-memory/`) are written by CI, which commits them to the PR branch, and never by an agent. A hand-edited `.claude/` file (`settings.json`, its hooks, a hand-written command or agent definition) changes only with the owner's explicit consent to that change: the agent shows the exact diff and the reason, asks first, and records the consent. Read before staging any path under `.claude/`.

What an instance OWES for every directory it declares — a visualiser, a documentation entry, a governing skill, json/jsonld/schema.json serialisations at the directory's URL and at every node beneath it, and a starting README of its own. Read before declaring a directory, before adding a graph typology, and when reading `check:subgraph-coverage`. Carries which obligations are ranked as unmet promises rather than unanswered questions, why the discriminator is "is this the static knowledge graph", and which single obligation a harness may never waive.
A tile is a function of the harness watching a directory, not of nodes. Where the tile set comes from, what a tile opens, and the two gaps it reports rather than hides.

While idle or waiting on a long-running async task (a build, a long compute script, a CI run, a background agent), pull the applicable backlog in priority order and work non-conflicting items instead of stalling. Use whenever blocked on an async wait with no substantive output to produce.

Rendering only what changed — seeding a build from a previous render, the two edges that decide what must re-run, why a step declares GRAPH TYPOLOGIES rather than paths, and the rule that could-not-determine always re-renders rather than serving a stale page.

`index.config.json` at an instantiation root says which harnesses the checkout instantiates, where each one comes from (local, or a remote mount pinned to a SHA), each instance's config INLINE in its entry (a legacy `<name>.config.json` is only imported until `--inline` retires it), and which harness `/` is. Covers instantiated against declared, landing resolution and its error case, `index.lock.json` and its legacy fallback, the reserved `index` stem, the generated `.gitignore` block and its gate, and `index-config:migrate` (with `--inline`) for separated repositories.

Where a value becomes program rather than data — workflow expressions, shell strings, and archive members. What the gate covers, why a step output carries a severity rather than having one, and the argv rule.

How to make a new KIND of harness instance — choosing the prefix family, the keep-the-kind's-name default and the owner's right to decline it, which inherited files the new owner may repoint, and what a new GRAPH typology must declare. Read before naming a new instance, before adding a value to the graph-typology registry, and before building a visualiser. Carries the test that usually says "this is not a new kind".

Every asset carries an id and a version and sits in DRAFT. Publication is a state, not a boolean, and `published` is refused by the schema because the formal process does not exist yet. Carries the id namespace rule, why a mirror never takes its subject's identity, and what a consumer may assume of a draft. Also the one home for which graph each instance publishes, where, under which IRI and schema, and what is stripped from it.

Sidecar-invalidation utility for the integration-watcher pipeline. Adds mechanical QA fields (script-reviewer entries) to per-block `.qa.json` sidecars and marks the existing entries stale so the next `qa-sweep` re-evaluates them. Use when a checker bug is fixed in a QA checker module (downstream "fresh" entries are now incorrect) or when a registry update adds a criterion the block hasn't been audited under.

Dispatcher for the `/integration-backlog <axes>` slash command. Works the backlog identified by the integration watchers (proof, canonical, compute, detangler, one-voice, …) by clustering the open findings into review-sized batches (≤ 49 files per PR — the reviewer-bot limit), proposing each batch to the author via structured AskUserQuestion calls, running `/prepare-merge` on each, resolving review comments (auto if mechanical, structured AskUserQuestion if architectural), then merging — and repeating until the axis is exhausted or the author signals stop. Sister command to `/integration-watch`: the watcher MONITORS for new events; this skill WORKS the backlog the watcher already catalogued.

Dispatcher for the `/integration-watch` slash command. Routes to one or more of the concrete integration watchers / audits (canonical, one-voice, consolidation, bibliography, devils-advocate, and those a content type's layer adds, …). With no argument, lists the available watchers and asks the user which to invoke. With arguments, dispatches the named watchers in parallel (each gets its own Monitor, queue, ledger, and PR-subscription set).

Abstract parent skill for domain-specific **integration watchers**. Encodes the shared mechanics — Monitor on `origin/main`, PR subscriptions, per-event QA dispatch, queue + ledger, idle backlog sweep, idle author-ask dispatcher, watch-PRs-you-prepare protocol, voice-pass on PR diff, witness-drift CI recovery, billing-quick-fail flake handling — that every concrete watcher inherits. Children fill nine domain-specific slots; everything else is shared here.

Establish how to talk to the person in front of you before deciding what to say — audio, ordinary chat, selectable options for limited hand function, large-type for low vision, plain language — and hold that choice durably so every later session and sibling agent honours it. Covers the accessibility rules a conversational agent can actually keep, the settings surface in the published site, and how to drive a question set from DMN so the SAME logic serves every modality. Use at first contact with a new user, when a user reports difficulty answering, whenever a question is about to be asked, and before any long free-text prompt.

Working a tracked issue — announce the branch when you create it rather than when you finish, and re-check the issue for new AND edited comments while you work. Both rules are about the gap between your view of an issue and everyone else's.

Journeys and workshops as knowledge-graph content: a DAK user scenario told as a journey map (`user-scenario` kind: ordered steps, per person what they do and feel, pain points, enablers, the record's trust state, and edges to stories, BPMN tasks, requirements, FHIR examples, building blocks and the DAK's data sets, decision tables and indicators), the `building-blocks` catalogue its steps use, a workshop that teaches from it (`workshop` kind: modules, objectives, questions for the room on each step, reference tables, sheets, job aids), the `journeys-viewer` visualiser that draws them for an instance and the layers it mounts, and the `check:journey-refs` gate that every reference they name resolves. Read before writing a journey or a workshop, before declaring the viewer, and before building a journey walkthrough app of your own.

The four affordances of a conformant knowledge graph — browse, materialise, instantiate and copy-into-folio — which capabilities each requires, how each writing verb degrades cleanly when no write capability is available, and how copying an asset stamps KgAsset.source provenance.

Ask whether agreed requirements should become knowledge-graph content, and as what — in a form the person can answer by selecting. Use at the end of CRDM sign-off, or whenever a body of agreed work could become a skill, a process, a schema or a work item and nobody has been asked. Offers "none" as a first-class answer.

Serialize an instance's knowledge graph to one JSON document, for publication and inspection. Read when asked to visualize, audit or share the KG, before adding a node type to the export, and before minting or authoring any subject IRI — subjects are `<doc dir>/<kind>/<id>`, never `#fragments`.

How a cold agent finds and loads the skill that governs its task. The two Tools that serve the knowledge graph — the MCP pair and the filesystem fallback — what counts as a skill, and the three ways the search goes wrong.

Separate a Knowledge Graph into its own repository — as a CONTENT repository (files to read, no code) and a TOOLS repository (the code that writes and checks it) — once it is too large, or its consumers or cadence differ. The end-to-end method: the signals that trigger it, the preconditions, eleven stages each with the command that gates it, the owner's decision points, how identifiers, QA and publication move, how the parent consumes the result, rollback, and the post-move sweep that a move between the pair owes before the parent re-pins. graph-detanglement owns stages 1–3; this skill owns the rest. Bootstrap + bootstrap-tools and cat-harness + the tools layer are the worked examples.

Lay out one declared sub-graph of a knowledge graph (a harness's schema overview, one named sub-graph, a declaration's kinds) as a single Graphviz diagram in the i2ce Form Documentor's convention, and show it on the site laid out in the reader's browser by Graphviz in WebAssembly, with pan, zoom, find, keyboard control and draggable nodes. The DOT is a third rendering of the model the PlantUML and Mermaid already draw, coloured from the same stylesheet. Tool `uml-overview`.

Subscribing a folio or harness to an external knowledge graph — a substrate — and walking its parts from referenced to materialised, one at a time and only through the shared materialisation gates. When to subscribe, what makes a repository a substrate, choosing subgraphs, assets and harnesses, the five gates, instantiating a harness so it reaches the navbar, moving the pin, and what never to do.

Getting a knowledge graph out to a public portal — the six stages between "the graph is in the repository" and "a reader's browser has the bytes", why a CDN is a layer rather than a publication host, and which decisions are the deployment's to make rather than the pipeline's.

Render a published knowledge-graph document so a person can read it — faceted index, node detail, followable edges, and an honest account of what the document is missing. Host-agnostic; the publishing is a separate Tool.

The BASIC ingestion flow every asset takes: an upload is accepted, its metadata goes into the knowledge graph, and the asset lands in `library/<slug>/` if it is materialized. The two entry points (a drop in `uploads/`, or materializing an asset a remote graph lists), what happens to the upload afterwards, and why content-type methods refine this flow from above rather than living in it. Command: `bun run cat ingest`.

Authoring a Liquid template in this repository — a README template the `subgraph-readmes` Tool renders with liquidjs, or a Jekyll include on the just-the-docs site. Where templates live (inside a declared directory, reached through its id), what a template may read (only what the Knowledge Graph hands it), the leading comment the generator reads as the file's description, includes, whitespace control, escaping, and regenerate-then-commit with the `--check` gate. Read it before adding or changing any `.liquid` file or anything under `docs/_includes/`.

Finding the source a node cites but does not hold — memory first, then this repository, then open-access services. Always produce a DIRECT download link. Read before recording that a citation cannot be found, and before appraising any source you have not opened. Its central rule: a blocked network is not a missing document, and the two must never share a report.

Build, read and audit a Latent Semantic Indexing index over a declared prose graph — a library, the skills, the work items, docs — to find units that discuss the same thing in different words, near-duplicates, outlier clusters, and a proposed home for unfiled work. Every output is a proposal; LSI never writes a relation.

After bootstrap, a person asks for part of a remote subgraph to be held locally. Check what is already here (cache:index), put a number on the ask before anything is fetched, then run materialize-remote. Eviction is a report, never an act.
Landing remote content locally — the five gates, the three states, and the two purposes. One process, shared by catalogue import and harness bootstrap, plus the refresh that is not a re-import.

Compose several Tool nodes into one MCP service — naming, collisions, grouping and versioning. Read when a service will expose more than one tool, or when two instances' tools land in the same namespace.

Verify an MCP service's tools against the Tool nodes and skill declarations they came from — I/O equivalence in both directions. Read before shipping a projected server, and when a tool call fails with an argument the schema said was fine.

Generate an MCP server from Tool nodes — the mapping from this harness's skill/Tool vocabulary onto the current MCP standard. Read before exposing a CLI tool over MCP, or when asked how an agent stands a service up.

Merge the base branch in and resolve, without a person, only the conflicts a DECLARED pattern covers — generated files, generated README regions, QA sidecars — then prove the result with the gate set. Refuses the whole merge when any conflict is authored or undeclared. Use for "merge main", "resolve the conflicts", "the PR is conflicted again", "auto-resolve", and when adding a pattern for a new kind of churn. Also governs what a merge steward does with a merge-train member it had to refuse: one deduplicated work item under the PR's own epic, a hand-back to the owning session with a fail condition, one dispatched agent when nobody owns it, one PR comment, and the close.

The merge manager agent's watch loop: what wakes it, how often it looks, how it tells whether it is the active merge manager, what it reads each time, which process each reading sends it to (merge train, saturation meta-merge, stalled-agent takeover), and how it keeps the swarm in step with hold and done broadcasts. Use for "be the merge manager", "watch the queue", "who merges", "the queue is stuck", and when starting or handing over the merge-steward lane.

Order the ready PRs and land them as a train: read each PR's live facts, let the reprioritisation table place it, merge the members together, run the gate set on the combination, and on red attribute and eject the culprit rather than reject the train. Every merge goes through `merge:guard`. Use for "merge the ready PRs", "land this PR", "what lands next", "run a merge train", "why was my PR ejected", "move this PR up", and when tuning the train's order or size.

Merging to `main` is its own step with its own gate: the `merge-to-main` sub-process, which every process that lands work CALLS rather than inlines. Covers the evidence read live on the head (CI per owed job, mergeability, review state, Claude Approvals where the repository runs it), why a repository with no CI is never green, who may authorise a merge and what does NOT count as authorisation ("fix all issues until green" does not), how the authorisation is recorded, and the post-merge steps: base green, site republished, downstream re-pins, work item and issue. Use for "merge it", "land this PR", "merge the green PRs", and before any write to a default branch in any repository.

How a named external methodology enters the knowledge graph, and how an agent picks which one applies. Read before following a judgement method, before adopting a new one, and before writing a house method instead of adopting one.

Three rules for any edit to a repository: make the smallest change that does the job and keep the diff minimal; read the repository's code-style files before writing code; and write Markdown without HTML tags. Use before writing a change and again when reviewing its diff.

How to execute audited SPARQL 1.1 named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads dataset distributions across CLI, MCP tools, and WebAssembly browser clients. Enforces graph availability guards to prevent silent partial results, and typed parameter bindings to eliminate SPARQL injection.

Judge whether the prose side of a declared prose ↔ code pair still says what the code does, when the machine could not settle it. Reads the two mechanical signals first — staleness and resolvable claims — and settles what is left in one of three ways, sending a disagreement with a checker to adjudication. General: the Lean case is a specialisation with its own skill.

Package, release, distribute, and retrieve Knowledge Graphs using npm tooling and tarballs: declare `package.json` as an authored pre-packaging asset in the Knowledge Graph, build `.tgz` packages via `bun pm pack`, record publications as `folio-binary-release/v1` state documents hosted on GitHub binary releases, and retrieve remote Knowledge Graphs using `npm install` for both unhydrated source graph and hydrated materialized graph views.

How to compile, partition by named subgraphs, and distribute W3C N-Quads datasets beside pre-compiled SPARQL 1.1 named queries for static edge and client-side querying. Enforces upstream skolemization for zero blank nodes, partition size budgets, and single-source-of-truth publishing via declared served directories.

One-voice integration watcher — watches origin/main + open active PRs + newly-opened PRs for content-block changes (`.md`, `.ts`, proof files), runs the per-block QA suite covering scholarly voice, AI-slop detection, section/chapter fit, canonical-vs-deprecated notation usage, and domain-boundary placement. Persists every finding to a sibling `<block>.qa.json` audit report (multi-reviewer, per-field SHA staleness). The watcher NEVER stops — when no events arrive it falls back to idle-sweep of the staleness backlog, rebuilding the audit knowledge base that feeds future content reviews. Inherits shared mechanics (Monitor, subscriptions, queue, ledger, idle sweep, author-ask, watch-prepared-PRs, witness-drift recovery, billing-quick-fail flake, sibling-PR comment protocol) from `integration-watcher`.
Author voice profile and narrative style guide. Reference when authoring or editing prose. Pairs with `one-voice-audit` (mechanical sweep for status leaks, emoji, and Unicode crashes).

Brief a work item or a topic BEFORE touching anything: what you are doing and why it is worth doing, what you already know and with what provenance, how you plan to do it and what would falsify the approach. Scales with irreversibility, not line count.

Cut a release of a repository's packages: decide the next version, write the release notes, tag, and create the release — for any repository, the platform or a folio. Publishing the built artefact to a registry is a separate, later step that a person starts.
Turning a value from outside into a path. The two different questions — a URL path versus a single identifier — why collapsing them is a defect, and how to find every sink that needs a check.

Show a published PDF inside a generated page — search, scroll, jump to page, print and download — with the pinned pdf.js viewer the site build installs. Which two Tools do it, the publication-gate rule that decides whether a page may embed a document at all, why the viewer opens only allowlisted hosts, and the three pdf.js behaviours that were measured rather than assumed. Read before putting a PDF on a page, before bumping the pdf.js pin, and when an embedded viewer shows an empty frame.
Show the current session's pending work — work items list + ledger intent. Read-only.

Pick up / continue work on one or more existing open PRs efficiently. Resolves each PR's REAL branch + title + checklist + reviews + CI in one batched pass, classifies CI as billing-vs-real, then dispatches one worktree sub-agent per PR with a filled-in brief, and applies the safe class of review-nit fixes (eval→ast.literal_eval, dead-code/unused-var removal, etc.). Use when the user says "pick up PR N", "continue 1543/1576/1571", "work these PRs", "address the review on PR N", or "take over PR N".

Establish where a new node belongs BEFORE you create it — which instance, which declared graph, which kind of node, and which of the two "stub" conventions applies. Read before adding a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision table, schema, tool or content object, and before writing any literal that names one folio.

`bun test` passing is not the gates passing. What to run before you push, why the list is derived from the CI workflow rather than written down, and what a `*:check` failure is actually telling you to do.

Write or update a pull request's description so that someone who has never seen the work can follow it: the problem, why it matters, how it was approached, what constrained it, the solution, how to use it, and what is not done. Read before opening a PR, before rewriting its body, and whenever the PR's scope changes.

Prepare for a handover: commit and push everything you hold, then write a handover report that cites the commits. Use it when told a stall, timeout or container loss is coming ("you may stall in N minutes"), before a long or risky step, or whenever a steward or the owner says "prepare for handover". It is the producing half; `handover-report` is the format and `stalled-agent-triage` is the reader.

Take a feature branch to a clean, conflict-free, green, pushed state so it can be merged with no surprises: base merged in, generated files regenerated, the folio's content-type gates run, then pushed. It does NOT merge and does NOT push to the default branch. Use for "prepare-merge", "make it mergeable", "ship it".

Full prepare-merge → resolve → merge pipeline. Coordinates with sibling PRs, resolves review comments, asks structured questions only when blocked, then hands the merge to the merge-to-main sub-process, which merges only on the owner's authorisation.

Track where you are inside a running process — which task, in which swimlane, under which role — and recover deliberately when you find yourself outside it. Read before completing a workflow step, and whenever something unexpected interrupts one. Covers what to do about notes and stickies you re-anchored while off-process, which leave no trace in the artefact.

Distinguish PRODUCTION (derived-only, no fits) from EXPLORATORY (empirical-fit probes OK as shape-hints) from NUMEROLOGY (post-hoc fits to known constants). The bright-line guide for which output goes where, the derivation-menu check, and the escalation path for off-menu coefficients, so empirical fits are not promoted into production scripts, "closed" status, dashboards or named constants.

Verify what a publish produced, and alert the publication manager whenever any step after the publish button fails — the verifier set, how to add a verifier, what is in scope, and how the publication manager triages the one alert.

Where a QA result lives now. Derived verdicts go to the orphan `qa-reports` branch, keyed by commit, written by the CI job `qa-publish`. Judgements stay on main in the `attestations` graph. Gates compute and judge against a stored baseline, and a missing one is unknown. Read before you regenerate, commit, resolve, cite or delete anything under `test/results/` or `test/attestations/`.

The QA projections written to `test/results/witnesses/` and stored on the `qa-reports` branch — what a `qa-witness/v1` document says, which three families produce one, how to read a verdict and the witness behind it, and why "could not determine" is a third state everywhere in them.

RACI over this repository's processes — who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each activity. Three declared edge kinds over the roles and BPMN activities that already exist, not a new party registry. Use it to work out involvement when a project is initiated, and to sketch its breakdown.

A folio's README is the author's file; the platform owns only the marked regions it generates. How the sync/audit split works, why the platform never generates a folio's prose, and the third state both tools must report.

Steward a WATCHED REF — a long-lived branch many processes write and one consumer serialises. Covers what makes a ref need a steward at all, why a coalescing window is a different object from a hold, the four durable fields a window needs so a handover cannot double-push, and the rule that a steward stores decisions and reads facts live. Use for "gh-pages is cancelling its own deployments", "two sessions pushed the same store branch", "who owns writes to this branch", "coalesce these pushes", and before giving any ref a concurrency policy.

Before new work takes shape, find the work it touches. Search work items, issues and open PRs for relevance; categorize and summarize every hit; then ask the user whether and how to coordinate. Judgement decides the categories and the recommendation, and the user decides the coordination. Called by CRDM when a requirement is initiated or updated in chat, and by methodology adoption. Process: sdlc/processes/related-work.bpmn.

Plan and track releases using work item epics. Covers epic creation, story/task decomposition, release readiness tracking, and the relationship between epics and GitHub milestones. Applies to code releases, paper publications, and project milestones.

Governs the release lifecycle: semver policy, draft/named releases, changelogs, release gating, and the relationship between feature branches, PRs, work items, and releases. Applies to code releases, paper publications, and project milestones. Complements package-release (which handles the mechanics of cutting a release) with the process and policy layer.

Bring a harness, and every instance it depends on, into a checkout that does not hold it, from another repository at a pinned commit, as declared directories with a lock: a `source.remote` entry in the downstream's root `index.config.json` (legacy: `remoteMounts` on its declaration) and `mountDefaults` on the harness. Covers when to mount and when to subscribe instead, why there are no submodules and no `.deps/`, the transitive closure through `needs` and gitlinks, overrides by id, the lock, and the three states.

Render a Knowledge Graph, or a list of its Subgraphs, for publication to a CDN at a publication root URL, and report a status and one message. The same step for a staging preview and for a release — only the root URL and the target differ. Names the target's Tool, never its steps: GitHub Pages (`gh-pages`) is one Tool, and it carries its own subprocess.

Log every render to the publish branch — what was published, removed, restored or deliberately retained — to an append-only log that lives beside what it describes. Use when adding or removing anything on `gh-pages`, when asking "what happened to this preview", or before writing a workflow step that deletes a published artefact.

The list of rendered files a Change Set alters, and how a reviewer approves against it. Each renderer maps the input files a change touched to the rendered files of its site through its dependency cone, before any build; a build diff then confirms the prediction. Use when opening or reviewing a Change Set PR, when asked "which pages does this change", when a prediction and a build disagree, or when adding a renderer.

Confirm a UI change by LOOKING at it in a browser and sending the screenshots to the author, rather than describing it. Use whenever a change touches CSS, a Liquid/HTML template, a generated page, the navbar, a board, a sticky or any rendered surface — before claiming it works, and before asking the author to review it. Covers building the site locally, taking the REAL CI build off `gh-pages` when the question is theme chrome or layout, driving it with Playwright in this environment, measuring computed style rather than reading the stylesheet, hit-testing a control's centre because visible is not usable, asserting the conditions so a check cannot pass over an unstyled page, and the defect classes that are invisible to a green gate set.

Lay folio-assistant over a repository that already exists, without losing or silently moving what is in it. Scans the tree read-only, classifies candidate files into library (external source) and content (authored here) with an explicit third bucket for what it cannot classify, scans outside the content tree for mathematical evidence and refutations, lists the content markers (an IG, a DAK, processes, work items, library, Lean, folio manifests) the harness could declare and declares only the ones the person picks, puts the three questions the scan cannot answer to the author as selections, and hands ingestion to one agent or a small swarm. Use when a user wants an existing repo converted to a folio, asks to import what is already there, asks whether their PDFs/notes/drafts can come along, or asks what else in a repository an existing harness could declare.

Every error gets a falling-off retry rate — each wait doubles, with jitter. Read before writing any call that can fail transiently, and before deciding that a failure is worth retrying at all. Exhausting the retries does not change the verdict.

The review page's heat map: a section-by-metric table that tells a reviewer of a large document where to look first. Says what each column MEANS and what it must NOT be read as, where each number comes from, what a column says when a build lacks its data, and how the colour was chosen. Use when a reviewer or author asks "where do I start", reads a number off the heat map, or asks why coverage or QA say "no data"; and before adding a column.

Actors, roles and skills — who performs a BPMN task, under which swimlane, with which skills. How a role's skill set is resolved through `inherits` and through a subprocess call chain, how a lane binds to a declared role, and how `kg:audit` finds a dangling skill, lane, role or decision.

Testing an import of a SAMPLE of a remote source into a knowledge graph or other structured store: scope it, let materialize-remote gate it, land it in the library (permanent) or the kept, unpublished trashcan (trial), import it, and test the import. The gates are called, never copied.

When the CI runners have been full for a long time, drain a repository's ready PRs in one step: hold the swarm, cancel the queued PR runs, stack every admitted PR onto one meta-merge branch with merge commits, and land that branch on `main` without waiting for CI, on the owner's card that names each PR. Then re-run main's checks and report. Use for "runners are full", "cancel everything and merge what's ready", "meta-merge", "consolidate the queue", and when the queue has not moved for an hour or more.

Manage a schema over its life — add one, change one, read the schema graph and its viewer, and act on what the reader could not determine. The layout rule lives in `directory-conventions`; the entity question lives in `data-modelling`; this is the work in between.

Adding, rotating and revoking the credentials the harness's automation needs, one mechanism at a time, with the exact GitHub UI path for each step. Every step that touches a value is a person's; an agent drafts the steps, checks names and expiry dates, and records what was done. Leads with the GitHub App on a personal account, the recommended mechanism.

The security sub-KG's entry point. What the boundaries are, which machinery already guards each one, and the single rule that unifies them — refuse, never repair. Read this before adding a check, so the answer that already exists is reused rather than rebuilt in a fourth place.

What a state machine tracks across a session, as against one process instance. What the record carries, why `actor` is required and the rest are not, why the session's view of a node is advisory, and what a sibling session reads it for.

Session-start intent declaration + session-end results recording, against the work plan's goals (milestone work items) and their open work items. Enforces the durable-handoff discipline so any agent can pick up another's thread.

An agent PLAYING a state machine rather than an engine executing one. Where the non-determinism actually lives, why the diagram stays strict, the `cat-harness.processes:judgement` marker that makes a judgement point countable, and what the machine must never do on the actor's behalf.

What any signature in the harness must answer, whatever it covers: who signs, what bytes are signed, which signature suites are accepted and who decides that, where the key is kept, which route signs (API or person, by reach), and what a verifier must check and record. Suites are named by the identifiers the standards already define. Signing is done by the parties' own systems; the harness verifies. Read before you add a signature slot, a trust anchor, a verifier, or a process that signs anything.

A visual fact — a colour, a glyph, a theme — lives in a graph node, and the stylesheet the site serves is a rendering of it. Read before adding a colour, an icon or a theme, before hand-editing any generated stylesheet, and before referencing a generated asset from a page.

Adding a skill is never a one-file change. What a new skill file owes, the one command that performs the derived half, the one declaration it deliberately leaves to you, why running it once is not enough, and the two orphan directions it reports rather than fixes. Read this before adding, renaming or removing a skill.

Reviews a skill against a voice that judges skills — the base `agent-skill-authoring` voice or a vendor override such as Claude's, Gemini CLI's or OpenAI's — rule by rule, with each rule's citation open, and records the verdicts with `voice:review`. Use when `skill-voice-review-current` reports a skill never reviewed or reviewed before the skill or the voice changed, or when asked whether a skill follows a vendor's authoring guidance. The agent half of that axis; the mechanical half, in `scripts/skill-voice-review.ts`, only says whether a current review exists.

A skill states a capability generically; a Tool node carries the concrete mechanism. Read before writing or editing any skill, and whenever a skill is about to name a vendor, a CLI, a binary or an API endpoint.

Spec-driven development, adopted whole: define what and why before deciding how, and do not develop before a spec exists. Carries what this platform adopts and — separately, with reasons — what it refuses.
The single declared template artefact for platform feature specifications, adopted from github/spec-kit. Mandatory sections and required fields are machine-readable here for automated validation.

When a diagram already says what the process is, the model should not be planning it. The two gaps between this repository's engine and a compiled control plane — typed node contracts and per-node context scope — what to do before either exists, and the three things not to adopt with the method.

Governs the lifecycle, syntax, and traceability of specifications and requirements across the harness. Connects spec-kit and CRDM tracks to the 6-part bootstrap Requirement definition, enforces EARS and ISO 29148 statement quality, and defines how requirements project to open standards (ReqIF, OSLC-RM) while keeping bootstrap strictly decoupled.

Staging preview and before/after comparison for content review. Takes one optional string — what the reader wants to look at, in their own words — and returns a list of URLs, each looked up in the publish ref, with what is published at it and what to review there. Provides before (MAIN) and after (branches/) pairs so reviewers can compare rather than guess. Used by the CRDM feature development workflow, content authoring review sessions, and whenever a staging preview deploys or someone asks to see it.

Triage incoming work from stalled agents. Given named agents or sessions, or a time window, find what they left (handover reports, open PRs, branches, work items, issue and PR discussions, workflow instances), collect as many handover reports as exist, reconstruct the rest, consolidate the workstreams into 2–4 themes, recommend how to fold them into the current or a new work plan, and coordinate open PRs with their owners (the merge steward above all). Use when a session or a swarm has stalled, timed out or lost its container, or when the owner says "pick up what X was doing".

A sub-KG is a knowledge graph staged as a directory inside a harnessed repository, declared as its own instance, that may later leave for a repository of its own. The lifecycle: declare it in place, grow it, stage it for separation (one import seam, the separation guard, a self-contained rehearsal), and then, each behind an explicit owner confirmation, create the repository, copy the staged contents in with history, re-point the declaration, verify on a fresh clone and delete the in-repo copy. The light sibling of kg-separation: use this for a DATA instance that leaves whole, and kg-separation when a graph must split into a content repository and a tools repository.

What was unexpected in that task, and does it belong in the corpus? Logical surprise is the detectable kind, recurrence is the filter that stops this generating noise every turn, and the agent PROMPTS — it never writes corpus guidance unasked.

Decide whether to run parallel agents at all, and if so how many, at which model level, against which decomposition. Read BEFORE dispatching more than one background agent — a swarm spends the author's tokens and the decision is theirs.

Running a SWOT situation analysis — the activities of `swot-analysis.bpmn`, what each step must produce, and the one thing the technique must never be used for. The method itself lives in the `methodology` graph and is not repeated here.

Recognize and respond to the three epistemic registers of author input — Socratic steer (known-answer correction), honest gap (flagged unknown), and intuition seed (tenuous cross-domain identification) — with the coactive-learning measurement spec (per-arc correction quality and turns-to-convergence) and the prompt-lexicon convention. Carries the STRICT rule that a steer correcting a RULE is written into the skill that governs it, in the same turn, quoted and dated — use whenever the author corrects, settles or overrules anything. Generic platform skill.

The check every BPMN task execution runs before anything is recorded: is the actor authenticated, assigned to the role the lane binds, authorized by an ODRL policy to perform the task, and allowed access to the content it acts on? One generic check in the engine rather than a step drawn in some diagrams; strict, with GitHub as the authenticator. Also how the HTTP routes ask the same policies. Triggers on: may this actor, who may perform, authorization, authentication, access rights, permission check, RBAC, rbac.ts, workflow_complete refused, not eligible for role.

Write and review technical documentation of standards, software and knowledge assets as an SDO writes. Carries the RFC 2119 requirement levels as RFC 8174 constrains them, the three questions a first draft is measured against, and the rule that an ingested specification is checked for supersession before it is cited.

When a glossary term the extractor minted and an authorised terminology disagree — the corpus spells a concept differently from the authority, or uses a word the authority does not carry — decide among three outcomes: change the prose, author a local term with its reason, or record that the vocabulary is wrong for this domain. Says which disagreements need a decision at all, how to choose, what each outcome writes and where, and what is NOT this skill (two judges disagreeing about a mapping).

Curating fixed (committed, cited, SME-reviewed) and generated (template + params + seed recipe, never stored materialised) test data sets in separately declared graph directories, with per-content-type specialisation as a called subprocess and attributable SME review of decision support and indicator definitions.

Run a `test-plan/v1` against a system under test and take it to a certification decision — the five lanes of `test-plan-execution.bpmn` (requester, tester, untainted checker, certifier, attestation service), how the test data is bound, what the run and the report must record, the facts the certification table reads, and the kg-audit criteria that judge a run afterwards. Read before executing a plan, re-executing a sample, or certifying a result.
Accept or refuse a set of three theme/avatar layouts arriving through document ingestion, with a named reason for every refusal.

The per-surface SPECIALISATION layer — sticky, landing board, docs background, navbar avatar. Only what DIFFERS lives here; the general rule lives in its stage. Read this last, after the stage that owns your question.

Why every scrim is measured over PURE BLACK rather than over the art actually in use, what the AAA floor is, and why the high-contrast pair declares no backdrop at all. The CONSUMER stage that says what the ink must survive.

What a theme IS as data — the palette, the three required layouts, and the per-image regions (`textRegion`, `avatarRegion`). The PRODUCER stage: this is where a number is written down, and the rule is that geometry over art is declared rather than derived, because no amount of arithmetic on an aspect ratio can see where a picture is quiet.

Turning a declared theme into CSS — `bun run cat themes:css` — and the single consumer-side failure this stage exists to stop: a theme with no CSS rule falls back to an opaque surface and paints over its own art.

Review graphical assets AS THEY ARE INGESTED, in the context of the website or app design they are for — accessibility, branding, languages — to determine what the assets and the UI will be. At ingestion only; called from ingest-theme. Measures rather than asserts, and raises findings rather than fixing them.

The map of this subgraph: theming is split on PIPELINE STAGE first — intake, declaration, generation, contrast — with producer/consumer as the direction each stage faces, and per-artefact specialisation last. Read this to find which stage owns the fact you need; read the stage for the fact.
Maintain and display work-in-progress task lists using the `beans` CLI issue tracker. Track implementation progress, open tasks, missing artifacts, and blocked items across a session.

Monitor and triage open feedback across all content blocks. At session start, ask the author if they'd like to work on feedback. Provide overview, let them pick a chapter/section, then review and iterate until done.

How concrete Tools are authored, structured, packaged, and registered across the separated multi-repository platform: defining Knowledge Graph Tool nodes, implementing TypeScript handlers in the tools repository, registering MCP tools, isolating toolchain dependencies, and validating tool-to-skill alignment.

Translation lifecycle management for folio content. Covers gettext PO/POT extraction and injection, TranslationNode manifests as KG nodes, official vs unofficial translations, staleness tracking, sign-off workflow, automatic badge rendering, and the poSources fallback resolution chain.

Say which work item you are on, every turn — the opening and closing report formats, the rules that make a report worth reading (two sentences and a link per work item, every mention), and the STRICT rule that the "next" line is a question and must carry its own context.

Move a path that other layers link to without making the order of their re-pins matter: the moving layer declares the move and keeps answering at the old path for a window, the dependent layers switch in any order, and the old path goes once nothing links to it. Use before moving or renaming a directory another layer links into.

Every user interface this project produces must be operable by keyboard, legible at measured contrast, and comfortable to hit. How to build to that, how to check it, why an automated pass is not the standard, and what a rendering built client-side owes a reader — there is no no-JavaScript floor here, and the two gates that look like one are narrower than their names.

Read, regenerate or extend the UML class diagrams of a harness: one per harness and one per named sub-graph it declares, plus the harness object model. Every box is generated from a declaration and a schema, never drawn by hand, so a wrong diagram is fixed at the declaration or the schema, and a dashed "could not determine" box is a finding about the registry.

The party that produced an artefact does not write the verdict on it. How a checker and an adjudicator are dispatched with controlled context, the three rules that make it a measurement rather than a ritual, and the third state that lets it gate at all.

Keep attacker-controlled values out of program text — in GitHub Actions, in command lines, in anything that is parsed before it runs. Read before interpolating any value into a script, and before giving a Tool a command-line input.

Never encode a constraint you have not verified — a rule that refuses a working setup is worse than no rule. Read before adding a check to a schema, a validator, a gate or an incompatibility table, and whenever you are about to write down that something "is not supported".

What an ingested file may be CALLED. Read before adding anything to an `uploads` or `library` graph, before writing a generator that links to one, and before "fixing" a broken link in a generated README. Covers which characters break what, why the name is normalised as well as the link escaped, how a sidecar stays paired with its source, and the one case the fixer refuses.

How a file actually REACHES `uploads/` — the two mechanisms that write bytes into a declared queue, the persona that performs one of them on somebody's behalf, and what each writer owes that the route does not do for them. The step before intake and after acquisition.
Notice what has landed in the acquisition queue, and tell an arrival from a backlog. Reports; it never deletes, and never ingests on its own say-so.

Watch a pinned upstream dependency for a new release, and take a candidate version through impact analysis, an MVP build, review and a person's adopt/hold/decline decision. Reusable per pin — the theme is the first tenant, not the only one.

Adjudicate `uses-editorial-completeness` — read a block as a reader would and judge whether its `uses[]` is complete and genuinely expository. The human/agent half of the `uses` QA axis; the mechanical half runs in `qa-checkers-uses.ts`.

Pictures of a changed figure, diagram or table, before and after, and how much of it changed. Says when to use it, what the percentage means and must NOT be read as, what a missing picture means, and how the staging job and the review process call it. Use when a reviewer asks "what does this figure look like now", when a table's markup diff is unreadable, or when a staging preview's pictures are missing.

The general strategy for a complex visualizer: the generated page carries identity, layout and a pointer, and its bulky or repeated content is fetched from the Knowledge Graph in the browser rather than baked into every page. What must stay server-side, how to fetch, how to stay equivalent to the render being replaced, and how to verify a page whose content is not in its HTML. Read before generating any page that shows a KG node's data at length: an IG artefact view, a graph viewer, a schema or sidecar view.

One vocabulary is authoritative for one kind of fact, and every other is a derived rendering reached by a declared mapping. Which vocabulary owns what here, the pros and cons behind each ruling, how DC and SKOS overlap and what stops them drifting, and the normalisation-first rule for any modelling or mapping exercise.

Load the active voices' rules BEFORE writing, so a block is drafted in the register it will be reviewed against. The authoring half of the voice overlay; `voice-overlay-review` is the half that runs after.

Adjudicate a `voice-*` finding — read the flagged passage as a reader of THAT genre would and decide whether the register is wrong, the criterion is out of scope, or the block is a stated exception. The human/agent half of the voice QA axis; the mechanical half runs in `qa-checkers-voice.ts`.

Review a block against the active voices' rules and record the verdict on its QA sidecar. The human/agent half of the voice overlay; the mechanical half is whatever `patterns` and `terminology` a rule carries.

Background-watch a branch (default origin/main) or a GitHub PR for new activity while you work, and on every event report whether to integrate / whether it conflicts with the current branch / whether it lets you simplify exposition / proofs / computations

The router for filing decisions. This repository answers "where does this go?" ten separate times; this says WHICH question you are asking, so an agent who does not know a rule exists can find it. One discriminating question per row, and the skill that owns the answer.

Design a user interface (a page, a visualiser, a navbar) by the WireGen methodology: a written design intent, at least two mid-fidelity HTML candidates, each with a web AND a mobile layout, mechanical checks at both viewports, a blind per-criterion review, adjudication where reviewers disagree, and a recorded choice. Also how an EXISTING visualiser is wireframed as-is, so that every declared visualiser has a wireframe with a QA sidecar. Process: processes/ui/wireframe-design-review.bpmn. Called for Design use from CRDM (Process_CRDM_Requirements, Call_Wireframe) whenever a requirement changes a rendered surface, before anything is built.

Render wireframe candidates at a web viewport (1280x800) and a mobile viewport (390x844), and record, per candidate and viewport, a pass or fail entry with a note for each mechanical criterion: renders, no-overflow, no-placeholder. Writes a screenshot per viewport beside the report. The mechanical step (step 3) of wireframe-design-review; a fail sends the candidate back to that skill's step 2.

Keep a short note on the work you are doing — what you did, what you decided and why, what is left open — with the memory tools, so the next person or agent to pick the work up starts where you stopped. Read when you are handed a piece of work, and before you stop working on it.

Reorganise a work plan that has outgrown one-bean-at-a-time repair — session logs typed as epics, duplicate families, generated template work items, stale claims, unparented work — through a reviewed PLAN rather than in bulk. The taxonomy is stated as data, a dry-run plan lists one row per work item (action, new parent, new status, evidence, note) with its before-state so the plan is its own inverse, the owner approves it by class or by row, and the apply is batched and reversible. Scrap, never delete. Read before changing the parent, type or status of more than a handful of work items at once.

The contract the work plan (work items) keeps as a data store, as operations any Tool must provide: get, list, create, update with ifMatch, note, history, and where a work item is in its processes. Give back a work item exactly as written, keep ids unique and links whole, keep status and type to their closed lists, lose nothing to concurrent writers, and answer a work item's history. A mechanical Actor plays this Role through whichever Tool the deployment names.

How the git state branch Tool performs the work-plan store's operations: the branch per graph, the mount at beans/, which command does get, list, create, update, note, history and positions, and how it keeps the race guarantee by fetching, rebuilding on the tip and pushing, never forcing. Read this only when the deployment's work-plan Tool is the git branch.

Where a running process keeps what it knows, and which store answers which question. The three records a step may touch, the one it may not, what `<cat-harness.processes:bean op>` actually performs, and why an instance and a work item must be one answer rather than two.

How this platform applies zero trust (the zero-trust-architecture methodology, NIST SP 800-207) to every hand-over between agents, skills, tools and graphs: rules H1-H9, the hand-over screen and where it is wired, the remote-mount trust gate, per-tool risk read from a tool's sinks, and the release security gate. A house application, not a methodology: read the node for the method, read this for what to do at a boundary.
